Cheers,

John

messages.subject_clean: Post-doc opportunity in Avian Conservation Ecology
messages.body_plain:
The Boreal Avian Modelling Project (BAM) is seeking an avian ecologist to fulfil a postdoctoral position at the University of Alberta. BAM is a continental scale effort to understand the ecology and dynamics of avian populations and their habitats in the boreal forest of North America (for more details on BAM see www.borealbirds.ca <http://www.borealbirds.ca>). Working with a team of avian ecologists, conservation scientists and statisticians, the post-doctoral fellow will conduct science to support the characterization and identification of critical habitat for several boreal bird species in Canada, including Canada Warbler, Olive-sided Flycatcher, and Common Nighthawk. The position will involve collaboration with federal and provincial governments, industry, and other academic institutions.

We are seeking a candidate meeting the following criteria:

1) Self-motivated & able to confidently interact with people of varying backgrounds
2) Strong background in avian ecology and conservation science
3) Knowledge of regulatory requirements related to migratory birds
4) Experience with wildlife-habitat modelling & Geographic Information Systems, preferably at large scales
5) Excellent and demonstrated writing skills
6) Strong quantitative skills

The position is available immediately. We will take accept applications until a suitable candidate is found. To apply, please provide a letter of interest, CV, and an example of your writing skills in the form of a peer-reviewed paper or thesis.

The position will be located at the University of Alberta in Edmonton, AB with an annual salary of $55,000 plus benefits. The length of the fellowship is 2.5 years.

http://wild49.biology.ualberta.ca/2016/09/12/post-doc-opportunity-in-avian-conservation-ecology/

Thanks for forwarding to suitable candidates and apologies for cross-postings.

Cheers,

Peter

Ecological Statistician – post-doctoral research position, 2 year renewable position, beginning fall 2016

To learn more or apply:  https://jobs.montana.edu/postings/5745

This is a non-tenure track, professional position that will work in collaboration with the US Geological Survey (Dr. Kathi Irvine), Montana State University (Dr. Andrea Litt), the National Park Service (Dr. Tom Rodhouse) and their partners to provide robust statistical inferences based on bat acoustic survey data. Results will provide information for the monitoring and conservation of North American bats.

The North American Bat Monitoring Program (NABat) has been developed to support coordinated monitoring of bat populations across North America. The monitoring program uses automated recording devices deployed for multiple nights. There is a need for guidance on the workflow for analyses of the resulting acoustic data as well as on how to account for species misidentification within occupancy models and how to properly account for the inherent uncertainty in the acoustic data.

The successful applicant will:

1.      Support NABat implementation and delivery by analyzing the acoustic survey pilot data that has been collected and take a lead in the following activities, as well as the resulting manuscripts and reports:

a.      Develop a work flow process for acoustic classifications of bat calls to species, which also identifies the possible sources of uncertainty. Workflow should account for multiple software options used for auto-classification, in addition to hand-vetting of call files. Summarize current knowledge and procedures used by NABat and their partners.

b.      Explore current Bayesian occupancy models to account for species classification errors based on acoustic data. Provide guidance on the use of such methods for practitioners, as applied to acoustic bat datasets with accompanying code and worked examples. Depending on the outcome of this work, develop an extension to current methodology, if necessary.

2.      Assist USGS and NPS, as needed, with developing guidance on master sample implementation of NABat.

Required Qualifications:

1.      PhD in Statistics or Ecology with statistics emphasis.

2.      Strong research experience in developing and applying Bayesian statistics.

3.      Understanding of occupancy modeling, sampling design and ecology.

4.      Documented success publishing in peer-reviewed literature.

Preferred Qualifications:

1.      Experience in ecological applications or at least some exposure to ecological fields of study or related course work.

2.      Previous experience with bat research and/or acoustic data a plus, but not required

3.      Excellent written and oral communication skills.

4.      A strong work ethic and the ability to work independently as well as collaborate with diverse partners and practitioners

Salary range of $40,000 to $45,000 annually, commensurate with experience, education, and qualifications.

To apply, please submit a cover letter and CV here:  https://jobs.montana.edu/postings/5745

messages.subject: Another Log Density/WAIC question
messages.subject_clean: Another Log Density/WAIC question
messages.body_plain:
Hi folks,

Another question related to WAIC and calculating the log posterior density using jags. A common way of coding, say, the occupancy likelihood in the BUGS language is something like:

z[i]~dbern(psi)
mu.p[i, j]<-z[i]*p[i, j]
y[i, j]~dbern(mu.p[i, j])

An alternative (now possible in JAGS 4.2) is something like:
z[i]~dbern(psi[i])
mu.p[i, j]<-psi[i]*p[i, j]
y[i, j]~dbern(mu.p[i, j])

WAIC is equivalent to -2 * log posterior density +2 pWAIC; the log posterior density can be estimated as

log.like[i, j]<-logdensity.bin(y[i, j], mu.p[i, j], 1)
lpd<-sum(log.like[])

and pWAIC is equivalent to the sum of the variance in each log.like across the number of simulations (vs. a Bayesian approximation to AIC; -2 * log posterior density +2K).

As one would expect, the log posterior density barely changes regardless of the formulation of the likelihood and the calculation of the lpd.  Also as one would expect, I think, when calculating WAIC using the conditional (first) form of the likelihood, pWAIC is much larger than when the marginal form of the likelihood is used (this version is approximately equal to AIC), and adding additional terms increases pWAIC yet further.  Just playing around a bit, the penalty for adding a single parameter is something like 50 units in some cases.  My sense is that the likelihood variance in y given z will always be  larger (or maybe much larger) than the variance in the likelihood of y given psi.  My questions are 1) whether the marginal formulation of the likelihood is more appropriate for calculating WAIC?, and 2) if the first question is true and one wants to make robust finite-sample inference, should one fit the model with both a marginal and conditional formulation?

Thanks for any feedback,

John

messages.body_plain: Should have done the proper reading/simulation first. For whatever it is worth, It appears that the marginal form of the log posterior density and the variance in the marginal form of the log-likelihood is more appropriate (is used by Broms et al 2016, although Hooten and Hobbs appear to use a conditional formlation), and using both marginal and conditional formulations (one for calculating derivations associated with z[i], one for estimating the log posterior density) easy enough to do within a single model.  Also, the final paragraph above appears embarrassingly incorrect: the conditional formulation not only tends to produce far lower estimates of pwaic, but also a much greater lpd estimate.

messages.subject: nonconvergence und estimation accuracy
messages.subject_clean: nonconvergence und estimation accuracy
messages.body_plain:
Dear list,

here's another observation on Rhat, and convergence and accuracy of estimates from an MCMC-based analysis. I used JAGS to fit a Poisson regression with two scales of temporal dynamics (within- and between-season) to data that were simulated according to the PH(enomenological) model for insect counts of Dennis et al. (JABES, 2015). In one version of the model, there were lots of parameters for between-year productivity (rho), date of peak flight period (mu) and width of flight period (sigma) that did not converge according to Rhat (and often dramatically so), and yet, the posterior means were astonishingly accurate ! In the attached Word file, you see part of the posterior summaries for the model fit to one data set and a plot of the estimates versus truth in the data simulation, with "perfect" estimates expected to sit right on top of the 1:1 line (the black line). Estimates from chains that have not converged according to Rhat are marked in red.

Please note that I am NOT saying that convergence monitoring is not important. Nor am I saying that we should use estimates from chains that have not converged according to Rhat or any other convergence test statistic. Normally, checking that Rhat is < than 1.1 or so is the very first thing that I do after an MCMC run and I would never publish results from an analysis that has key parameters with a greater value of Rhat or if I did I felt not very at ease (and would clearly declare so in the Methods or the Results section). But what I am saying is that there is more to convergence monitoring than simply looking at Rhat < 1.1 that perhaps, if you have run an analysis for 2 weeks and Rhat is still not below 1.1, you may just take what you have (but declare what you do openly).

Comments welcome.

Best regards  --  Marc

Hi all,

I suppose this question best fits in chapter 3 of AHM but uses ch. 10. I am fitting a model set of single-season occ. models across several species, a set which includes a global model (a model including all explanatory variables - which, btw, are all continuous). I have two species with very similar detection histories:

Species 1: detected at 40 / 150 sites, 481 zeros, 54 ones

Species 2: detected at 51/150 sites, 462 zeros, 73 ones

The global model for species 1 fit with no fusses:

    var7 + var13 + var8 + var9 + var10 +

    var11 + var12, data = umf)

(Intercept)   -0.1550 0.414 -0.3748   0.708

var1          -0.0297 0.342 -0.0869   0.931

messages.subject_clean: Question about GLM: NaNs produced in global model
messages.body_plain:
Hi Brent,

That can have something to do with the detection histories of species 1 and 2. In some cases the correlation between variables and detection histories is such, that correlations between variables don't have an effect on the models.

In my work I sometimes had the case that species with a high number of detections (generalists) were harder to fit with a large number of variables. For species with less detections, many variables didn't have any effect on psi, largely due to the fact that when a species would have a detection at a location X, other locations with a detection would have fairly similar e.g. landcover characteristics, i.e. similar variables values.

That's just one possible explanation and really just anecdotal from working with 'messy' data before. There is probably other, more analytical explanations, that others might be able to offer.

Cheers,
Richard

You are welcome. I struggled with this quite a bit too when I started
using occu. The way how I dealt with this sometimes was to create lists
of occu models and remove the ones that were nonsensical or did not
converge. I wrote a function for this (f.AICc.occu.sig) and am attaching
the function source script as well as a really simple example R script
in case you are interested.

I have used this here:
http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1600-0587.2012.07681.x/full
and here:
http://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0099292
although the technical information is a bit limited in both.

Cheers,
Richard
